items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.
items.t: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
items.t: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

items.title: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind
items.summary:
When the humpback got stranded on Germany’s Baltic coast, crowds gathered, conspiracy theorists pitted themselves against scientists and animal lovers argued with vets. Why did the animal trigger such an intense derangement?

What surprised Bodo Köpnick was how loud the whale was. “You could hear it as far away as the next village. It was eerie, but also impressive,” he says, then pauses to think how best to describe the noise a suffering humpback makes at night. “It was like a cow moaning. It went to your marrow.”

Köpnick, 65, is everything you would hope for in a volunteer fire chief on a sleepy holiday island: a grandfatherly figure who mostly spends his weekends teaching local children about health and safety, and letting them climb on the engines. But on 31 March his life was made infinitely more stressful by the appearance of a lost whale that had got itself stranded on the shores of his island of Poel, in northern Germany. It became his fate to stand on the shoreline and guard the huge creature while behind him an entire country lost its mind.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘People couldn’t deal with watching an animal die’: the strange saga of Timmy the whale – and how a whole country lost its mind

items.title: ‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers
items.summary:
A heatwave in the Bering Sea that killed 10bn snow crabs has led to a new hybrid emerging that has no fishing quotas

Somewhere out on the Bering Sea, hundreds of miles off the coast of Alaska, a group of researchers onboard the trawler Alaska Knight haul up a heap of crabs from the seabed. As they sort and measure their haul, something seems wrong.

The catch, which usually features species such as the snow crab – a species of spider crab growing up to a metre wide with its legs outstretched – or its larger relative, the tanner crab, is instead dominated by an odd-looking hybrid of the two species.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Legally, they don’t exist’: the hybrid crabs puzzling biologists and fishers

items.title: The British island that made a deal with nature
items.summary: LUNDY ISLAND — United Kingdom. Out in the Bristol Channel, nestled between Wales and England, the rugged island of Lundy is one of the UK’s most pioneering conservation stories. From the return of thousands of seabirds to thriving marine life beneath its waves, decades of conservation have helped transform this small island. But Lundy’s story isn’t simply about keeping people out. Local fishermen helped shape the marine protected area, and the UK’s first ever no-take zone was designed alongside the needs of the people who depend on these waters. Today, the island is home to thriving wildlife, a working fishing community and thousands of visitors each year. Mongabay’s Video Team wants to cover questions and topics that matter to you. Are there any inspiring people, urgent issues, or local stories that you’d like us to cover? We want to hear from you. Be a part of our reporting process—get in touch with us here! items.title: Country diary: Watching a garden spider at work – do I detect a personality? | Oliver Southall
items.summary:
Hurstpierpoint, West Sussex: The way that it sits patiently, and solves problems … it’s hard not to wonder if it has some kind of inner life

Three months with a newborn has given me a fresh perspective on nature. What will Tom enjoy out here, I wonder, as we step outside. I hold him under trees and watch his astonished eyes. Every morning, as a hopeful inoculation against arachnophobia, I show him the garden spider (Araneus diadematus) outside our back window. Is that a smile?

Attending to a baby’s developing preferences has got me thinking about what makes an individual creature unique. Recently I learned that Len Howard – whose 1952 book Birds As Individuals lovingly described the quirks of her garden tits and thrushes – lived nearby. Contemporary experiments with honeybees have shown that diversity in workers’ personality traits makes for an adaptable and resilient hive.

Continue reading...

items.title: Extreme rainfalls flood Sri Lanka’s coastal city as wetlands, drains vanish
items.summary: COLOMBO — On Nov. 6, a 129-millimeter (5-inch) downpour flooded parts of Sri Lanka’s commercial capital within minutes, stranding commuters and submerging a large number of vehicles. Siva Sivasagunthan, a three-wheeler driver working at a local ride-hailing app, told Mongabay that the water levels quickly increased and his vehicle was partially submerged in water. It took him around two hours to reach a location that would have usually taken 30 minutes to reach on a normal day. The downpour left many Colombo residents panicking. According to Ajith Wijemanna, director of Sri Lanka’s Department of Meteorology, there have been a few instances over the decades when Colombo has experienced rainfall exceeding 400 mm (15.7 in). In June 1992, the city experienced a rainfall of 493.7 mm (19.4 in). In November 2010, a 440.2 mm (17.3 in) rainfall was recorded in 24 hours. Wijemanna told Mongabay that the intensity of the rainfall — the speed of rainfall received in an hour — is extremely important. According to meteorological department readings, the rainfall intensity on Nov. 6 was more than 120 mm (4.7 in) per hour. The rain gauge reading at another location in Colombo indicated more than 135 mm (5.3 in) of rainfall per hour. “We believe that the main cause of flooding was the high intensity during a short period of time, such as an hour, which was similar to a gushing downpour,” Wijemanna said. He noted that Sri Lanka currently lacked technology such as a Doppler radar system to support…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Extreme rainfalls flood Sri Lanka’s coastal city as wetlands, drains vanish

items.title: Autopsy Results Reveal What Really Happened To Fiona The Hippo, As Witnesses Speak Out On Freak Accident
items.summary:
The autopsy results for Fiona the hippo have finally been released, giving more details about what happened inside her body after she swallowed a visitor’s knitted hat. 

The nine-year-old Cincinnati Zoo favorite passed away on November 19, despite her caretakers trying several ways to save her. 

Now, the zoo has shared the findings of her examination, explaining why the veterinary team couldn’t remove the object and why even continued treatment wouldn’t have changed the outcome. 

Autopsy results revealed how the hat became stuck inside Fiona and couldn’t be removed 

On Friday, November 20, Cincinnati Zoo released the results of Fiona’s necropsy, the term for an animal autopsy. 

The examination revealed that the knitted hat had become lodged in the middle of her small intestine . It was approximately 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines. 

This meant the object was stuck in a part of her digestive system the veterinary team could not reach with the equipment available. 

Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden / Youtube 

We are so appreciative of all the outpouring of love that we’ve seen from our community and wanted to share an update on what was found after a necropsy was performed on Fiona.

items.title: US leases American Samoan seabed for mining in auction deemed illegal by court
items.summary: The U.S. government has auctioned off 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of the American Samoan seabed, despite public opposition and a federal court ruling that found the sale to be illegal. The sale marks the first time a country has completed an auction of seabed mineral leases that grant the right to explore for minerals. The auction, which took place on the morning of Nov. 19 in Thousand Oaks, California, was publicly livestreamed, offering two vast lots of American Samoan seabed: One covering about 15 million acres, and the other about 16 million acres. Mongabay attended the livestream. Just two bidders showed up: A U.S. company called Wetstone U.S. Ventures and the Norwegian company Adepth. However, only Wetstone participated in the bidding process. By the end of the auction, which lasted approximately 20 minutes, Wetstone had secured both leases at the starting price of $3 million each, equivalent to approximately 19 U.S. cents per acre. In 2024, American Samoa, a U.S. territory, imposed a moratorium on deep-sea mining in waters extending up to 3 nautical miles from its coastline. The U.S. government has jurisdiction over the remainder of the exclusive economic zone (EEZ), which extends 200 nautical miles from shore, allowing it to pursue seabed mineral activities in this area without approval from the American Samoan government. Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, center, and other activists protesting outside the site of the auction in Thousand Oaks, California. Image by Hunter Ries/Greenpeace USA. In a statement released on Nov. 16, a few days…This article was…
items.t: US leases American Samoan seabed for mining in auction deemed illegal by court

items.title: Striking snakes released into the wild in historic fight to save species from extinction
items.summary:
Scientists reared the San Francisco natives through their vulnerable youth before setting them free in nature

San Francisco garter snakes born and raised in a zoo-based conservation program have been released into the wild for the first time as part of an effort to save what is considered one of North America’s most beautiful snakes.

The non-venomous reptiles are known for their striking colors – red heads, turquoise bellies and vibrant red and black stripes on their sides. The species, found only on the San Francisco peninsula, has been listed as endangered for more than half a century.

items.t: Striking snakes released into the wild in historic fight to save species from extinction

items.title: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects
items.summary: For many people a trip to the zoo is an opportunity to see favorite animals like gorillas, giraffes and lions. But in Alburquerque, New Mexico, U.S., visitors can add spiders, scorpions and ants to their must-see list at the ABQ BioPark BUGarium. The facility also includes an aquarium, traditional zoo and botanic garden. The BUGarium was closed for a year and reopened in October 2026 following a $1.45 million renovation. Insects are the largest group of animals on Earth, and ecologically essential as pollinators and the base of many food chains. Famed entomologist E.O. Wilson once said: “If we were to wipe out insects alone — just that group alone — on this planet, which we are trying hard to do, the rest of life and humanity with it would mostly disappear from the land. And within a few months.” The BUGarium exists to educate the public about the importance of insects. “Whether they’re pollinating plants, recycling nutrients, controlling pests, or supporting entire food webs, these animals are essential to healthy ecosystems,” said ABQ BioPark Associate Director Matthew Peterson in a statement. Bugs are not always an easy sell. “Guests come to the BUGarium with a wide spectrum of attitudes ranging from disgust and horror to fascination and awe,” Alexandra Miller, the curator of entomology at the ABQ BioPark told Mongabay in an email. “We hope guests learn how important arthropods are to ecosystems around the world, what they can do to support native populations, and that arthropods require specialized care…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Renovated BUGarium in the US aims to connect people and insects

items.title: Philippine corn farmers investigate links between chemical farming and soil erosion
items.summary: LAKE SEBU, Philippines — To the untrained eye, a handful of soil might appear to be a monotone brown. But to farmer Welna Sumulde, who grew up among generations of Indigenous T’boli farmers on the Philippines island of Mindanao, the slightest change in the color of the soil is a whisper from the land, a warning of its degradation. “Around 2023, we observed changes in our soil. The color became lighter, the leaves looked different, and the cassava we harvest became smaller. We also observed fewer living organisms on our soil,” Samulde told Mongabay. Samulde and other farmers in her community also thought changes in the soil might hold answers to a troubling puzzle: Why do fish keep dying in nearby Lake Sebu, a lake that lies in the natural basin below their upland farms? They said they began to suspect that soil erosion from surrounding corn farms was speeding up siltation in the lake — and that changes in farming practices were accelerating erosion. With the help of NGOs and scientists, the farmers were able to test this hypothesis. MASIPAG Mindanao coordinator Leo XL Fuentes, in yellow, conducts a soil test alongside farmers of the Lem Bulul Farmers Association. The farmers are comparing soil fertility and pH between traditional and chemical corn farms. Image by Geela Garcia for Mongabay. Corn-fed culture Although rice is the core of the Philippine diet, corn is the primary agricultural crop of Lake Sebu; a 2021 study found that 53% of the municipality’s agricultural…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Philippine corn farmers investigate links between chemical farming and soil erosion

items.title: Story Of Fiona And Her Dedicated Caretaker Breaks Hearts Around The World As Fans Mourn Famous Hippo
items.summary:
A child’s visit to the Cincinnati Zoo on November 8 took an alarming turn for one of its best-known residents, Fiona the hippo. 

The nine-year-old animal swallowed a knitted hat thrown into her enclosure by the young guest, leaving her in need of round-the-clock supervision as caretakers tried to help her pass the foreign object naturally. 

Unfortunately, efforts to help her overcome the complications proved unsuccessful, and Fiona passed away on Thursday, November 19, after experiencing a loss of appetite and dehydration. 

The news has since sparked an outpouring of tributes, with many also expressing sympathy for the people who cared for her, particularly Jenna , who had been by her side since infancy. 

“This is devastating for her,” one X user wrote. 

Netizens express condolences as Jenna’s lifelong bond with the nine-year-old hippo draws attention 

Indiana University Alumni Association 

Cincinnati Zoo caretakers, alongside a team of veterinary experts, attempted a colposcopy on Fiona and had her stand on a vibrating plate in an effort to help her pass the hat. 

Jenna appeared emotional in one of the videos shared by the facility as it kept fans updated on the hippo’s condition. 

When the zoo eventually announced that Fiona had not survived, Jenna was among the first people many online commenters thought about. 

An X user named Amunet, who shares commentary on entertainment and culture, highlighted the bond between the two and asked people to send the caregiver their love as she navigates the loss. 

“Jenna was with Fiona her entire life. My heart breaks.…
items.t: Story Of Fiona And Her Dedicated Caretaker Breaks Hearts Around The World As Fans Mourn Famous Hippo

items.title: Indigenous protesters board soy and oil barges on Brazilian Amazon river
items.summary: Hundreds of Indigenous protesters on several small boats and canoes stopped and boarded barges carrying soybeans and fuel on Brazil’s Tapajós River in the eastern Amazon. The demonstrations on Nov. 14 and 15 were to demand protection for the river amid industrial expansion and legal recognition of Indigenous territories in the region. The two-day demonstration near Santarém, in Pará state, drew more than 650 protesters. “Our children need this river, just as we need this river,” Jackson Tapajós, executive secretary of the Tupinambá Indigenous Council who participated in the protest, told Mongabay by phone. Smoke in the air from nearby forest fires was so thick that protesters could not see the barges approach until they were close, he said. Indigenous women negotiated with armed security guards after approaching the fuel barge on Nov. 14, explaining that the group was peacefully protesting. The guards allowed them to board but stayed with them, Tapajós told Mongabay. “We managed to talk to some of these guards … but they were by our side the whole time, the whole time with their guns, so that creates a lot of tension,” Tapajós said. The Tapajós River is an export artery for the region, carrying large amounts of soybeans and corn from Brazil’s agricultural heartland to ports on the Amazon River, which ultimately connect to international trade routes via the Atlantic. According to the Ministry of Ports and Airports, 16.8 million metric tons of cargo was moved through the waterway in 2025, up 14.3% from 2024.…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Indigenous protesters board soy and oil barges on Brazilian Amazon river

items.title: It’s time to put Africa’s forest communities on the map (commentary)
items.summary: The U.N. General Assembly’s recent adoption of a new standard world map, more accurately reflecting the true size of Africa than depicted in the Eurocentric 16th-century Mercator projection, is great news and a welcome reminder that multilateralism isn’t dead yet. It also doesn’t tell the whole story. We’re not talking about how the continent was carved up between the former colonial powers through such events as the Berlin conference of 1884-1885, though the social, economic and political impacts of the often straight and artificial lines drawn on those maps are still felt today. No, we’re talking about how maps of Central African states are still used by foreign interests and political elites as tools to perpetuate power — with control of natural resources and the benefits they generate tending to flow outwards and upwards — rather than to the people living in these areas. Resource map of the Congo Basin. Graphic courtesy of Earth Insight. Today, much of the Congo Basin, the world’s second largest rainforest, resembles a patchwork of extractive industry concessions, strictly protected areas and an ever-increasing array of carbon offset projects which our organization has documented. These have largely failed to stem deforestation and biodiversity loss, while delivering few or no benefits to local populations, and in many cases, causing severe impacts on human rights and food security. What maps typically don’t show are the systems of longstanding customary rights and usage by Indigenous and local communities (IPLCs) that extend across the vast region, and which…
items.t: It’s time to put Africa’s forest communities on the map (commentary)

items.title: Where family foundations can help marine conservation
items.summary: COP17 ended in Armenia amid disappointment over the lack of concrete measures to reduce biodiversity loss by 2030. Finance was a sore point. Philanthropy is only a small part of that picture, but foundations can take risks that public agencies often cannot. I think there are some particularly good opportunities for smaller foundations in marine conservation. My intended audience is family foundations that give away perhaps $2 million to $15 million a year and have a handful of staff. Over the summer I went through the academic literature and Mongabay’s coverage in English, Spanish, and Portuguese to see what the evidence actually shows about marine conservation outcomes in the Americas. A first summary of that assessment – “From paper parks to lasting protection, here’s what works in marine conservation” – appeared last month. In some cases Mongabay’s reporting helped me understand why the results of a study were so disappointing. Our reporters had spoken to the people responsible for managing these areas, as well as people who lived or fished in them. In reading about some of these places, I was struck by how long the laws protecting them had been on the books. Some of the agencies responsible for enforcing those laws lack adequate funding. Elsewhere, the designation of a protected area was done with little regard for the people who fished there. A school of mobula rays off Mexico. Image by Rhett Ayers Butler Making existing protected areas work I suspect it’s easier to raise money to establish…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Where family foundations can help marine conservation

items.title: Ecuador copper mine advancing despite opposition from Indigenous communities
items.summary: A proposed copper mine on Indigenous land in southeastern Ecuador is getting closer to opening despite opposition from some Shuar communities, who say they reject the project altogether and don’t want to participate in talks with the government. The Warintza mine received environmental authorization this year, and officials will now begin meeting with Indigenous communities about how the project, if constructed, would impact their way of life. But some community members don’t want to be consulted at all, and say they’re worried about relocation from the territory. “We want absolutely nothing to do with mining,” one community member, who asked to remain anonymous due to fear for his personal safety, told Mongabay. “And we don’t even want to be consulted.” If the project moves forward, Lowell Mineral Exploration Ecuador S.A., a subsidiary of Solaris Resources, would extract copper for around 22 years from approximately 8,660 hectares (21,399 acres) across six concessions. It would also extract molybdenum concentrates and some gold and silver. A soccer game in the center of the Maikiuaints community. Image by Brandi Morin/Survival International. Construction would clear more than 2,025 hectares (5,003 acres) of primary forest and divert the Warints and Piuntz rivers, critical to Indigenous communities’ way of life, according to the environmental impact assessment, which received technical approval in April. It could irreversibly change the landscape in some places even after the mine is closed, the assessment said. Surface water and groundwater quality also face high risk,…
items.t: Ecuador copper mine advancing despite opposition from Indigenous communities

items.title: Could a short tail mean a new monkey species in Laos? Some scientists think so
items.summary: There is no body. No genetic evidence — yet. There are just photos, but some scientists say those photos show a distinct enough primate to declare it a new species: the short-tailed langur, or Trachypithecus brevicaudus. The proposed species was described in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology and lives in the Annamite Mountains of Laos. “A photograph of a langur, published by the Saola Foundation, caught my attention because the animal’s tail is noticeably shorter than that of any other species within this group of limestone langurs,” said Tilo Nadler, lead author of the paper and a wildlife consultant for the Vietnamese government and various NGOs. This photo led Nadler and colleagues to investigate. They traveled to the area, a remote set of limestone karsts in Bolikhamxai province in central Laos, and took their own photos. “The first time I observed a group of these langurs, it was immediately clear to me that they were different from all the other limestone langurs I had previously encountered and knew well,” Nadler told Mongabay in an email interview. “It was a very exciting experience.” Male short-tailed langur of a group. Image by Tilo Nadler. But not all scientists agree that these photos prove a new-to-science species. “It could well be a new species, but I think the data that have been presented do not give sufficient support for this,” said primate expert Vincent Nijman, director of EcoVerde Global Consulting, who wasn’t involved with the paper. But Nadler said the encounter, and photos,…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Could a short tail mean a new monkey species in Laos? Some scientists think so

items.title: Quechua community in Peru builds up Andean bear camera trap project on their own reserve
items.summary: Maribel Pacco grins as she recalls the first time she saw an Andean bear close-up in the wild. At the forest edge, a mother and her cubs browsed on bromeliads while the volunteer ranger watched for hours in awe. “I’m not a biologist, but at that moment, I decided to become a conservationist,” she says. Today, Pacco leads a camera-trap project to estimate bear numbers and movements in Pumataki, a private community-owned reserve in the buffer zone of Manu National Park, in southeastern Peru. With the help of her Indigenous Quechua community of Pillco Grande, the project has generated some of the first local records of Andean bears (Tremarctos ornatus) in Pumataki. So far, they have identified 10 individual Andean bears, distinguishable by the unique pattern of facial markings. Though modest and only 3 years old, information gathered from the camera traps helps inform a Quechua-language environmental education program for youth and is shared at community meetings to highlight the area’s biodiversity. “In the last few years, I’ve seen a lot more involvement of women in Andean bear conservation which is fantastic to see,” said Rebecca Zug, a professor of biology at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito, who is not involved in the project. “There is also so much more power in Indigenous communities building conservation from within and learning about their own biodiversity from someone like Maribel than in having an outside voice come in.” For now, limited funding has forced the project to scale back some of…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Quechua community in Peru builds up Andean bear camera trap project on their own reserve

items.title: UN climate talks slammed by activists, leaders as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft agreement
items.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year’s U.N. climate summit reaches its final day. Friday marks the official end of this year’s two-week summit, known as COP31, which so far has failed to advance the drastic emission cuts needed to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change. Negotiators in Turkey expect the talks to go into overtime on Saturday. Civil society groups have warned this year’s summit runs the risk of being the “worst COP ever” if fossil fuels don’t make it into the final agreement. By Suzan Fraser, Anton L. Dlegado, Sibi Arasu and Victoria Milko, Associated Press Banner image: Attendees walk near a warning that reads “don’t fall for fossil fuels” at the COP31 U.N. Climate Summit, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Image courtesy of Khalil Hamra, Associated PressThis article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: UN climate talks slammed by activists, leaders as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft agreement

items.title: Japan looks to offshore wind to boost energy security, but hurdles remain
items.summary: Japan has “tremendous potential” for offshore wind power, according to the national government and experts. But achieving that potential means overcoming major hurdles. While commercial-scale projects began coming online in recent years, the country still needs to address challenges that include refining its public-private partnerships, a buildout of related industries (such as turbine production), and involving local communities. However, tapping into offshore wind as a primary sustainable domestic energy source is critical to Japan, with the country’s energy self-sufficiency rate standing at just 16.4% in fiscal year 2024. The country’s first commercial offshore wind farms came online in Akita prefecture, at the ports of Noshiro and Akita, in 2022 and 2023 respectively. These wind farms, along with others that have come online since, currently generate 0.5 gigawatts of electricity, with capacity for a total of 5.7 GW by March 2031 if projects currently in the pipeline proceed as planned. But the nascent industry remains in its infancy. “Japan’s offshore wind power policy is currently at a very important turning point,” notes a team of experts from the Renewable Energy Institute (REI), a Japanese think tank. A fixed-bottom offshore wind turbine at Japan’s Akita Port in 2022. Image by 掬茶 via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Offshore wind milestones and millstones The government stands fully committed to offshore wind: Recent milestones include the passage of legislation in 2025 opening up Japan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ) to wind farm development. The nation’s EEZ,…
items.t: Japan looks to offshore wind to boost energy security, but hurdles remain

items.title: Floating wind is building ‘A lot of momentum’ toward commercialization
items.summary: It’s a little-known, nascent sustainable technology on the verge of commercialization: Floating wind turbines deployed across deep ocean waters could unlock vast amounts of renewable energy in the coming decades. For some countries (including China, Japan, South Korea, the U.K. and EU), floating wind is already playing a role in plans to decarbonize national economies, owing either to a lack of viable fixed-bottom offshore wind sites, or due to limited space for land-based renewables. For now, the emerging floating wind industry consists chiefly of small-scale demonstration and pilot projects, totaling around 300 megawatts (MW) of global output, a capacity dwarfed by current worldwide fixed wind generation at nearly 100 gigawatts (GW). The largest floating wind farm currently is Hywind Tampen in Norway with 11 floating turbines producing 94.6 MW for use by oil and gas installations. Despite its current lack of scale, Louise Efthimiou, the floating offshore wind manager at World Forum Offshore Wind, still sees floating wind “as a very strong contender” for decarbonization, albeit on a smaller scale than fixed offshore sites. “We can acknowledge that floating wind will not necessarily represent the bulk of offshore wind,” she told Mongabay in a video interview. “But it does benefit markets who don’t have the choice to do other than floating wind … offshore because of their water depths and their environment.” The major hurdle is getting floating wind up and running at a commercial scale. “The technology works, but it’s still in a phase of innovation, and so that…This…
items.t: Floating wind is building ‘A lot of momentum’ toward commercialization

items.title: Last Javan rhino habitat caught between mining plans and relocation debate
items.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesian lawmakers and environmental groups are urging the government to revoke a mining map covering part of the waters around Ujung Kulon National Park, home to the world’s last surviving Javan rhinos. The calls were in response to a proposal by Hashim Djojohadikusumo, a mining and energy tycoon and the brother of President Prabowo Subianto, to move some Javan rhinos (Rhinoceros sondaicus) from Ujung Kulon at the western tip of Java to Alas Purwo National Park at the other end of the island. Hashim made the statement during the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Türkiye on Nov. 12, in his role as the Indonesian government’s special envoy for climate and energy. He cited natural disasters as a major threat to the species, making the need for a translocation necessary. “If there is a tsunami due to an earthquake or a volcanic eruption, our Javan rhinos can go extinct,” he said. The national park is located around 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Anak Krakatau, a highly active volcano in the Sunda Strait that’s the remnant of the famous Krakatau. An eruption in December 2018 sheared off part of the slope of Anak Krakatua, leading to a landslide that triggered a tsunami. The waves radiated to Java and Sumatra, killing more than 420 people on both islands. None of the 68 rhinos at Ujung Kulon were affected, it was reported at the time. President Prabowo Subianto, right, confers a civilian honor on his brother, Hashim Djojohadikusumo, at the State Palace…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.t: Last Javan rhino habitat caught between mining plans and relocation debate

items.title: How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
items.summary:
The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground. The Guardian has examined dozens of satellite images and spoken to environmental experts in an effort to assess the scale of the damage

items.title: One in four land reptiles depends on rock habitats. Lack of protection leaves them in a hard place
items.summary: More than a quarter of the world’s land reptiles depend on rocky habitats, yet these areas are often overlooked in conservation efforts, according to a recent study. For cold-blooded lizards, snakes, and worm lizards (legless lizards), rocks often provide warmth for basking, shelter from predators, and places to hunt, socialize, and breed. However, the number of reptile species globally that use rocky habitats like cliffs, outcrops, or karst systems, and how threatened they are, still remains uncertain, researchers write in the study. To fill the gap, the researchers analyzed 9,729 terrestrial species belonging to the order Squamata, which includes all lizards, snakes, and worm lizards. For each species, they consulted the IUCN Red List, which documents its conservation status, habitat requirements, and threats. Their analysis found that 2,479 species, or more than 25% of those studied, use rocky habitats. Of these, 1,022 species, or 10.5%, were entirely dependent on rocks — that is, they lived almost exclusively on rocks and used rocks for breeding, shelter, and to regulate their temperature. Of the studied species that use rocks, nearly 30%, or 676 species, are classified as threatened on the IUCN Red List, the study found. Species that depend entirely on rocky habitats were 51% more likely to be critically endangered than those that use them only occasionally. items.t: One in four land reptiles depends on rock habitats. Lack of protection leaves them in a hard place

items.title: Fossil fuels’ role in Africa’s energy transition contested as UN climate conference closes
items.summary: As the 2026 edition of the annual U.N. Climate Change Conference reaches its conclusion in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 20, African governments are arguing for increased financial and technical support to respond to climate change. Top priorities include more money for protection of forests and other landscapes, funding to help vulnerable communities and economies adapt to a changed climate, and financial backing for a just energy transition for fossil-fuel producing and consuming economies on the continent. Access to energy and what role remains for fossil fuels are contested topics, with many African governments planning continued reliance on coal, diesel and natural gas for transport, industry and electricity generation. Jane Mbabazi Byaruhanga, responsible for environmental and social affairs at Uganda’s Petroleum Authority, is among the thousands attending the summit. Africa’s households, schools, health centers and businesses lack access to affordable, reliable energy, she told Mongabay in a phone interview from Antalya. Two in five Ugandans lacked access to electricity from the national grid in 2025, according to government records; in rural areas, access was 43% of the population. This situation is mirrored across the continent: The International Energy Agency estimates that nearly 600 million of the continent’s 1.5 billion inhabitants do not have access to electricity. “Africa, to begin with, needs reliable and affordable energy to enhance their development, and we should always aim at the continent to have energy that is produced and also used responsibly,” she…
items.t: Fossil fuels’ role in Africa’s energy transition contested as UN climate conference closes

items.title: Nickel linked to deforestation in Indonesia traded on London Metal Exchange, says report
items.summary: Two companies approved for trading nickel on the London Metal Exchange (LME) could be linked to supply chains that have cleared primary rainforest in Indonesia, according to a report published by the NGO Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). The NGO investigated two LME-approved Indonesian refiners – PT CNGR Ding Xing and PT Eternal Nickel Industry (ENI) – and traced each of their corporate ownerships to mines driving extensive deforestation across Sulawesi and the North Maluku islands. The investigation claims  that the companies’ supply chains were possibly linked to clearing up to 7,270 hectares (17,965 acres) of primary rainforest in Indonesia. Current LME rules require metal brands to comply with the OECD’s Due Diligence Guidelines, which provide government-backed management recommendations for “responsible supply chains of all minerals”, including their refined metal derivatives. However, the guidelines lack binding environmental criteria for deforestation, biodiversity loss or Indigenous land rights, according to the EIA.  “The LME has put in place solid requirements on metal sellers to address supply chain issues like conflict financing and child labour,” said Colin Robertson, EIA Forests Campaign lead for mining, told Mongabay over email. “Deforestation caused by mining is a growing problem and it seems to be a blind spot for the LME and for the mining and metals sector in general.” Neither company  publicly discloses its mine suppliers under current LMEpassport rules, the digital platform for recording and sharing information about the physical metal that…
items.t: Nickel linked to deforestation in Indonesia traded on London Metal Exchange, says report

items.title: As Nepal celebrates the crow, urban sprawl and waste drive strain
items.summary: Every year around the Hindu festival of Diwali, or Deepavali, residents in Nepal observe Kaag Tihar, an annual festival day dedicated to worshipping house crows as divine messengers. However, in the country’s capital, rapid urban sprawl, habitat degradation and changing perceptions toward the bird are testing human-crow relations, reports Mongabay’s Gobinda Pokharel. Satellite analysis shows Kathmandu’s urban build-up area expanded by 124% between 1989 and 2018, while another study found municipal green space plummeted by 54% between 1975 and 2025. Meanwhile, the removal of more than 2,000 mature trees along major thoroughfares like the Kathmandu Ring Road has forced house crows (Corvus splendens) to nest on utility poles and electrical wires, according to a 2024 study led by Tribhuvan University researcher Dinesh Bhusal, in Nepal. “When old and large trees are cut down, specialist birds lose their habitats,” said Hem Bahadur Katuwal, a bird ecologist at the Xishuangbanna Tropical Botanical Garden, Chinese Academy of Sciences, southwest China. “Eventually, only functional generalist species, such as crows, which can survive under almost any conditions, remain.” Compounding the population shift is Kathmandu’s unmanaged refuse. Open dumping of waste along riverbanks and uncovered trash at meat shops provide abundant forage, attracting dense concentrations of crows and black kites (Milvus migrans). “Large quantities of discarded food and exposed waste from meat shops have contributed to the unusual increase in crows and kites in Kathmandu,” said Kamal Raj Gosai, an…
items.t: As Nepal celebrates the crow, urban sprawl and waste drive strain

items.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
items.summary: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

items.title: The long reach of El Niño impacts on Southeast Asia’s primates
items.summary: As Indonesia’s El-Niño driven fires spark a race to save endangered orangutans and other wildlife, a recent review paper, published in the journal Oryx, is raising concerns about both the short- and long-term impacts on primates of such climatic events in Southeast Asia. “Primates might survive a fire, but that doesn’t necessarily tell us whether they’re going to have enough food or suitable habitat, or what’s happening with their health and ability to reproduce in the months and years ahead,” said Elizabeth Barrow, lead author of the paper and conservation research director at the Gunung Palung Orangutan Conservation Program (GPOCP), Indonesia. With 94% of Southeast Asia’s primates threatened with extinction, the impact of El Niño is a poorly understood but significant threat to populations, according to the researchers. “From my perspective, this is a huge conservation issue for primates in Southeast Asia,” Barrow said. Habitat loss and degradation caused by drought and fire are linked to several concerning impacts. They can drive changes in diet, behavior and the physical condition of primates, the review found. Primate populations can become crowded as forest areas shrink, while others may be displaced, suffer localized extirpations, or increased infant mortality. In total, however, the review identified only 15 papers on the impacts of El Niño-linked drought, fire and smoke on primates. Research was limited to just seven of 105 primate species, and entirely focused on Indonesia, leaving major knowledge gaps. “Although there are very few papers, the effects on primates…
items.t: The long reach of El Niño impacts on Southeast Asia’s primates

items.title: Catching more plastic than fish in Sierra Leone’s coastal Mahera
items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — On a rainy Saturday morning, 57-year-old fisher Sheriff Kamara sat among other community members inside a wooden makeshift shelter in Sierra Leone’s Mahera Beach, waiting for the weather to improve. Along the shoreline, discarded plastic bottles, water sachets, bags and food wrappers lay scattered among old footwear and foam. For Kamara, plastic waste has become a regular problem, increasingly affecting his ability to fish and earn a living. “When I started fishing, it was rare to find anything in my net besides fish. But now, it is a weekly, sometimes a daily, problem,” he tells Mongabay. According to Kamara, a lot of single-use plastic waste frequently gets caught in his fishing nets, particularly near the shore after a heavy rain. Removing the entangled plastic waste takes considerable time and effort. “I find all sorts of plastic in my net almost every week. Removing the plastics with my apprentice’s help takes a lot of time,” he says. For fishermen like him, plastic pollution is not just an environmental concern but an additional burden on their daily work and livelihoods. To support the fishing communities, the government launched a fisheries and marine resources strategy in 2025, which provides a 10-year framework for promoting sustainable fisheries management, protecting marine ecosystems and improving livelihoods. It also calls for sustainable use of marine resources and stronger protection for the fisheries sector. Plastic waste, including discarded bottles and containers, accumulated along the shoreline beneath fishing boats. Image by…
items.t: Catching more plastic than fish in Sierra Leone’s coastal Mahera

items.title: Peruvian officials reportedly increase tally to more than 12,000 tarantulas in recent seizure
items.summary: Peruvian authorities have updated the number of tarantulas seized in a recent wildlife trafficking case from 3,000 to more than 12,000, according to South American media reports. The final count of 12,796 seized spiders was reportedly announced by the Peruvian National Police (PNP). The authorities said they believe these arachnids are worth more than half a million euros (around $548,000) on the international market. On Nov. 4, 2026, the Peruvian National Forest and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) announced it seized thousands of tarantulas at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima, hidden inside socks and plastic containers in luggage destined for Germany. Authorities arrested two German citizens and a Polish national, including a “renowned tarantula researcher” who was not publicly identified, and detained them for further investigation at the time. The seized tarantulas included individuals in different life stages, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, and came from across Peru. They included blue bird eaters (Thrixopelma lagunas), Bolivian blue leg bird eater (Pamphobeteus antinous), members of the genus Pamphobeteus  and several newly described species. Authorities said the alleged traffickers collected the spiders from the wild to sell as exotic pets to collectors and for research. None of the seized species are internationally protected under CITES, the global wildlife treaty. However, they are protected nationally under Peruvian laws, and removing them from the wild is an offense. In a TV program, General José Manuel Cruz Chamba from the PNP reportedly identified one…
items.t: Peruvian officials reportedly increase tally to more than 12,000 tarantulas in recent seizure

items.title: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says
items.summary: The International Energy Agency reports that the energy shock from the Iran war is reshaping global energy strategies. Released Thursday, the report highlights how countries are prioritizing energy security and affordability, benefiting renewable technologies like solar and nuclear power. The IEA warns that the crisis’s effects will deepen the longer it lasts. At the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, electrification and reducing fossil fuel reliance are key issues. The IEA projects a decrease in oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz and an increase in solar and nuclear power. Energy demand for cooling has overtaken heating for the first time this year. By Anton L. Delgado and Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Banner image: People walk near solar panels at a photovoltaic power station operated by Huadian (Beijing) New Energy Development Co. items.t: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says

items.title: In Sri Lanka, human actions are driving wild animals into cities and suburbs
items.summary: COLOMBO – It was a surprise for Mohamed Fareed, a resident of Jawatte, an upscale neighborhood in Sri Lanka’s commercial capital Colombo, to find a peacock near his house back in 2020. Today, there are at least 12 peacocks, including peahens roaming the area. “In the mornings and evenings, we hear their loud and piercing calls and now the neighborhood is used to their presence,” he told Mongabay. “Sometimes we see them on rooftops. Children are quite excited to see them. These peacocks frequent the area near the mosque to feed on pigeon feed inside the Jawatte mosque.” Peacocks have been frequently spotted in densely populated areas such as Kollupitiya and Mount Lavinia and, similar to Fareed, many residents are seeing peacocks near their home for the first time in their lives, and the numbers are increasing. items.t: In Sri Lanka, human actions are driving wild animals into cities and suburbs

items.title: “Rooting For Her”: Cincinnati Zoo Updates Public On Fiona The Hippo After She Swallowed A Child’s Knitted Hat
items.summary:

Fiona , the beloved nine-year-old hippo whose premature birth and remarkable survival captured hearts around the world in 2017, swallowed a knitted item thrown into her enclosure by the young guest. 

What initially appeared to be something the animal might overcome without difficulty has since developed into a more concerning situation, with her appetite beginning to decline and raising concerns among her veterinary team. 

As specialists explore ways to help Fiona pass the object naturally, her caregivers have turned to an unconventional piece of equipment in the hope of aiding her recovery. 

Zookeepers try an unusual recovery method as beloved hippo remains under close veterinary watch

In a video update shared by the zoo on November 17, a member of the veterinary staff explained that they had expected the relatively small object to pass through her digestive system.

items.title: Geopolitical tensions hamper efforts to curb overfishing in waters near Europe
items.summary: LONDON — On Nov. 10, Mongabay went to the site of the annual meeting of the body that regulates fishing in the northeastern Atlantic, where a little-known geopolitical dispute over marine resources was playing out behind closed doors. The North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC), a multilateral body, governs the fishing of three major stocks of fish in international waters near Europe, as well as associated species and habitats. Disagreement between countries over how to manage the stocks has had serious consequences, experts say. All three species — Atlantic mackerel (Scomber scombrus), Atlanto-Scandian herring (Clupea harengus), and blue whiting (Micromesistius poutassou) — have been subject to overfishing for years. The Northeast Atlantic mackerel population is in particularly bad shape, currently 22% below the NEAFC’s target threshold, having been fished above scientifically advised levels every year since 2008. The NEAFC is one of the world’s 17 regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs), and a fisheries governance campaigner has called it the most “fraught” and “problematic.” It has six member parties: the European Union, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Norway, Russia, and Denmark (on behalf of the Faroe Islands and Greenland; the delegation is commonly called DFG). The three fish species are prey for marine mammals and seabirds, and are sought after on global markets. Mackerel is sold in tins, herring is eaten pickled or smoked, and blue whiting is used for aquaculture feed. At this year’s annual meeting, held Nov. 10-13 in London, the parties made no…
items.t: Geopolitical tensions hamper efforts to curb overfishing in waters near Europe

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.
items.t: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
items.t: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.
items.t: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

items.title: Britain’s birds stay closer to home amid mild winters
items.summary:
Smaller species such as swallows and skylarks are more likely to stay near breeding grounds rather than migrate

Bonfire Night is over, Christmas is coming, and Britain’s birds are getting ready for the winter. They must survive the extremes of our weather and make it through to next spring to get the chance to breed again.

Birds have very different strategies to prepare for cold weather. Many smaller birds – swallows and swifts, cuckoos and chats, warblers and flycatchers – simply avoid it by migrating: some fly all the way to sub-Saharan Africa, where they enjoy the benefits of a second spring and summer south of the equator. Others, such as blackbirds and robins, stay put. But if they sense that a cold spell is coming, they too will head south, though not as far – most either remain in south-west Britain or cross the Channel to France or Spain.

items.title: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia
items.summary:
Scientists use lightweight tracker to map wading bird’s extraordinary migration from Norfolk to the Arctic and back

A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first UK mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant.

A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird. Populations that visit Britain spend summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter. In 2022, one bar-tailed godwit made the longest recorded non-stop flight, 13,560km over 11 days from Alaska to Tasmania.

items.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
items.summary: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

items.title: UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds
items.summary:
Populations at lowest level on record with 45% of native breeding species in decline, environment watchdog says

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are breaking the law by failing to intervene to slow the “deeply concerning” decline of Britain’s wild birds, the UK’s environment regulator has said.

New data shows that wild bird populations have dropped to their lowest level on record, with almost half – 45% – of 132 native breeding species in decline over a five-year period.

items.title: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs
items.summary:
Scientists and fishers study how these ‘reefs’ and the creatures living on them are transforming the ocean floor – and what it means for the fishing industry

A few years ago, Tony DiLernia, a New York-based charter boat captain, heard rumors of prime fishing near the Block Island windfarm, off the tip of Long Island. So he went with his family to see for himself. Almost immediately after motoring up to one of the project’s five turbines, black sea bass and summer flounder started nibbling at his rod and reel.

DiLernia, who has fished for 50 years, wasn’t surprised: he knew about the reef effect, where certain species cluster around structures like the turbines. “It’s what we call ‘stupid fishing’,” he joked. “You’ve got this thousand-foot [signpost] sticking up out of the water saying: ‘Fish here.’”

items.title: ‘When it roars, we roar back’: the man who faces Bengal tigers armed only with a stick
items.summary:
Abdul Goni Gazi fainted with fear during his first big cat encounter but now his mission is to help them coexist with people

At the age of 15, Abdul Goni Gazi had an experience that would alter the course of his life. It began as a fishing trip with his brother, deep within the Sundarbans, a vast landscape of mangrove forest, rivers and islands stretching across the tidal delta of Bangladesh and India.

“We went to the riverbank to cut firewood for cooking,” he says. “I was standing there holding the boat in place, while looking towards the bank.”

items.title: Country diary: Thrilling views of Iceland’s humpbacks, (perhaps) lured in by Céline Dion | Claire Stares
items.summary:
Eyjafjörður: Our boat was surrounded by around 15 of them, exploding their exhalations out of the water – and numbers are increasing here

For the first half-hour, Eyjafjörður, Iceland’s longest fjord, offered few signs of marine life – just three cormorants and a raft of common eiders. Then, suddenly, there it was. A distant spout of water vapour. A humpback whale.

As we motored out, more bushy plumes appeared to port and starboard, until we found the boat surrounded by about 15 individuals. Cutting the engine, the captain announced that he was about to employ a secret technique to coax the whales closer. There were raised eyebrows as the opening notes of Céline Dion’s My Heart Will Go On crackled over the speakers. But, as if on cue, two explosive exhalations erupted alongside the boat, prompting whoops of delight.

items.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
items.summary: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.
